query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A conventional, impurity‐controlled low‐alloy ferritic steel will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition when subjected to systematic tempering treatments, because at intermediate tempering temperatures impurity elements (e.g., phosphorus) segregate to the grain boundaries, inducing temper embrittlement—a phenomenon not observed in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional low‐alloy (ferritic) steel with a well‐defined chemical composition and controlled impurity content, initially having a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematic heat-treatment (tempering) at incremental temperatures spanning below, within, and above the narrow temper embrittlement window (e.g., 300°C, 400°C, 500°C, and 600°C).
generation.conditions: The experiment is carried out under controlled conditions with identical alloy batches, ensuring steady cooling rates and performing tensile and fracture toughness tests at each tempering temperature. A comparative treatment on high‐entropy alloys (which do not exhibit temper embrittlement) serves as a baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: The segregation of embrittling impurities (such as phosphorus) to the grain boundaries during tempering triggers the transition in mechanical behavior.
generation.mechanism: At lower tempering temperatures, the microstructure retains ductility; as temperature increases to an intermediate range, impurity segregation to grain boundaries causes a reduction in ductility (brittle behavior); further increase in temperature leads to re-dissolution or diffusion of these impurities away from the boundaries, restoring ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The low‐alloy steel will show high ductility at low tempering temperatures, a significant drop in ductility (increased brittleness) within a narrow intermediate temperature range, and a recovery of ductility at higher tempering temperatures. In contrast, high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys will not exhibit this dramatic ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
generation.baseline: The absence of temper embrittlement in high‐entropy alloys under similar heat treatments.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected only in conventional alloys with controlled impurity levels; alloys with high compositional complexity are predicted to be immune to such a transition.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature ranges for the transition and the magnitude of ductility loss/recovery may vary depending on the precise impurity levels and microstructural factors, requiring detailed experimental characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of conventional low‐alloy ferritic steel samples with controlled impurity levels. Subject the samples to tempering at a series of temperatures that span below, within, and above the suspected temper embrittlement range (e.g., 300°C, 400°C, 500°C, and 600°C). Conduct systematic tensile tests, fracture toughness measurements, and microstructural examinations (using microscopy and spectroscopy to assess grain boundary impurity segregation). In parallel, perform the same heat treatments on a high‐entropy alloy sample that serves as a comparison.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the conventional low‐alloy steel does not display a statistically significant drop in ductility at intermediate tempering temperatures compared to lower and higher temperatures, or if the trend (ductile–brittle–ductile) is similar to that observed for the high‐entropy alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.conditions: a conventional low‐alloy steel of well‐defined chemistry and impurity level, subjected to a series of controlled tempering treatments covering the low, intermediate (embrittled) and high temperature regimes
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by deliberately reproducing the well‐known ductile–brittle–ductile transition found in conventional alloys. By controlling the tempering temperature, the study isolates the mechanism of temper embrittlement, contrasting it with the absence of such a transition in compositionally complex/high‐entropy alloys, which is central to understanding why chemical complexity prevents the phenomenon.
